title: Thrust — King of Attacks: Sword and Buckler
subtitle: Petr Vasiliev’s seminar in Istanbul on stance, independent hand work, counterattacks with opposition, and thrusts at different levels.
source_name: Workshop Thrust is a king of strikes
note: The seminar is conducted primarily in English. The summary, semantic structure, and full transcript are presented in English.
overview_theses: In sword and buckler fencing, the two hands must be able to act independently and then come together again in a coordinated attack or defense.
Stance and body coordination are not ends in themselves: they give both hands room to move without unnecessary repositioning.
The high defensive potential of sword and buckler makes a simple attack less reliable and increases the value of a counterattack with opposition.
The buckler should be directed toward the opponent’s blade and attacking line, rather than simply punching forward or pressing into the opponent’s shoulder.
An inside-line thrust depends on changing the grip, rotating the wrist, moving the body, and preserving space for the point.
A short half-step invitation can provoke a buckler reaction and open the upper line for a prepared thrust.
A thrust to the torso can reach farther than a cut to the leg and change the score faster, but it still requires preparation and distance control.

chapters.title: Organizing the Training Space and Equipment
chapters.summary: The group lines up, clears working space, and prepares swords and bucklers before the main topic begins.
chapters.anchor: Let's go, line up.
theses: Each participant needs roughly one step of space forward and backward.
Swords and bucklers are first placed nearby so the stance can be introduced without weapons.

chapters.title: Why the Thrust Matters in Sword and Buckler
chapters.summary: The instructor introduces the seminar topic and connects the value of the thrust to the use of two independently controlled weapons.
chapters.anchor: Okay, so today's topic is the best strike is a thrust.
theses: In sword and buckler, mastering the thrust is treated as a more important foundation than practicing cuts alone.
Independent control of sword and buckler expands the range of simple and compound actions.
Bringing the hands together can sometimes be useful, but participants first learn to control them independently.

chapters.title: A Stance for Independent Hand Work
chapters.summary: Participants adjust an overly side-on stance into a more frontal one so both hands and the torso can move more freely.
chapters.anchor: And we start with very simple exercise.
theses: A stance designed for a single weapon limits the potential of the buckler hand.
A slight turn of the torso and weight on the balls of the feet make it easier to change sides without losing tempo.
The weapon position should establish a direction rather than force the blade to travel around its own guard.

chapters.title: Coordinating the Hands and Body
chapters.summary: A basic drill connects stepping, separating the hands, and rotating the torso before transferring the movement to weapon work.
chapters.anchor: Let's do exercise.
theses: During a forward step, one hand extends while the other compensates by moving back.
The wrists and pelvis rotate with the motion as parts of one elliptical path.
In fencing, the action is not isolated in the arms: the whole body contributes.

chapters.title: Defensive Potential of Different Weapons
chapters.summary: By comparing saber, rapier, longsword, and sword and buckler, the instructor explains why the preferred action depends on the weapon.
chapters.anchor: Ozgen, come closer.
theses: Saber requires active footwork because a defensive mistake can quickly lead to a hit.
A thrust depends on a precise point line: even a small deviation can make the action miss.
Sword and buckler provide two independent defensive tools that can close different target areas.

chapters.title: Counterattack with Opposition
chapters.summary: Instead of a long exchange of parries and ripostes, the attacker is met with a simultaneous thrust covered by the buckler.
chapters.anchor: before we land uh to the to the topic to the thrusts
theses: A simple attack against two defensive tools often gets caught in a series of parries and ripostes.
Inviting the attack makes the opponent’s timing more predictable.
A counterattack with opposition combines the hit and closure of the line in one tempo.

chapters.title: Buckler Surfaces and Defensive Angles
chapters.summary: The instructor shows how to receive the blade with the working surface of the buckler rather than the fist, using an extended arm and a suitable angle.
chapters.anchor: don't worry uh we continue at the same pairs
theses: A buckler has no long, powerful lever, so it should not try to overpower the blade through leverage.
The blade is caught between the flat and sloped surfaces while the arm stays extended.
Wrist pronation and the direction of the incoming attack help establish a stable angle.

chapters.title: Distance and Footwork in Defense
chapters.summary: Footwork is added back to the hand actions: stepping back with the parry and moving forward with the counterattack preserve safe distance.
chapters.anchor: We forget about arguably the most important part of fencing
theses: Parrying in place leaves the legs exposed and allows the opponent to keep pressing.
A half-step back is often enough to receive the attack and preserve room for the riposte.
Moving forward during the counterattack supports both opposition and thrusting distance.

chapters.title: Unusual Thrusting Angles
chapters.summary: Before putting on full protective gear, participants explore less familiar angles that complement standard thrusting mechanics.
chapters.anchor: important concepts without them uh it's hard for you
theses: Unusual angles do not replace basic mechanics; they depend on them.
The instructor distinguishes his experimental material from standard rapier practice.
The group puts on protective equipment before the more contact-intensive section.

chapters.title: Half-Step and Space for the Riposte
chapters.summary: A response to a question clarifies when to stay in place, when to retreat, and why a thrust needs free space.
chapters.anchor: yes that's uh that's the point because uh
theses: If the distance already suits a counterattack, the fencer can act from the spot and then exit.
During a conventional parry, a half-step back prevents the opponent from maintaining uninterrupted pressure.
At very close distance, torso thrusts are restricted and only close-range options remain.

chapters.title: Thrusting Against Repeated Power Attacks
chapters.summary: Using HMB fighters as an example, the instructor explains why a central thrust is useful against pressure, repeated attacks, and strong lateral defense.
chapters.anchor: we have our comrades HMB
theses: Stopping after the first contact is dangerous against an opponent who continues attacking.
A strong lateral defense does not always protect the central line of the torso equally well.
A direct thrust requires precise distance, so the next section introduces a variation that needs less space.

chapters.title: Thrusting Along the Buckler’s Inside Line
chapters.summary: Participants practice an inside-line thrust resembling an imbroccata by rotating the wrist, changing the grip, and moving the body around the defense.
chapters.anchor: And that's what we're going to learn first.
theses: An intermediate grip of roughly 45 degrees makes it easier to transition between cutting and thrusting actions.
The action begins not with arm extension alone, but with the arm and body entering inward together.
The blade is brought toward the inside of the buckler and the thrust is completed with a step.

chapters.title: Freedom of Movement with an Extended Arm
chapters.summary: Two grip options are compared to show how mobility in the shoulder, elbow, and wrist expands the available thrusting angles.
chapters.anchor: We have two opinions on how to thrust properly.
theses: The instructor does not declare one grip uniquely correct and explicitly notes the lack of evidence.
An extended arm with a mobile wrist provides more degrees of freedom for changing the line.
The drill aims to maintain blade control while moving the buckler without losing protection.

chapters.title: Where to Direct Buckler Pressure
chapters.summary: In response to a question, the buckler is directed into the blade rather than the shoulder to limit the opponent’s continuations and allow a safe exit after the thrust.
chapters.anchor: So what happens?
theses: Pressure into the shoulder may be prohibited by the rules and does not guarantee weapon control.
Controlling the blade temporarily reduces the opponent’s available lines for a response.
After the thrust, the fencer should pass quickly or withdraw because attacks to the legs remain available.

chapters.title: Continuing the Thrust Up the Inside Line
chapters.summary: The inside-line thrust continues upward so the sword and buckler alternately cover the sides, head, and legs.
chapters.anchor: Let's see the next exercise.
theses: A direct thrust with an extended arm remains the foundation, but it does not cover every sword-and-buckler situation.
Moving inward helps block the opponent’s blade and close under cover.
The buckler covers one side, distance protects the legs, and the sword covers the other side and the head.

chapters.title: Parry-Riposte and Counterattack
chapters.summary: The same mechanics are practiced first as a parry-riposte and then as a counterattack moving forward.
chapters.anchor: Now let's go for the tactical situation
theses: During the parry-riposte, the body compresses on the retreat and then opens into the thrust.
During the counterattack, the same structure is performed while moving forward as the hands and body separate along safe lines.
Participants are advised to begin with a controlled parry-riposte to understand the angle before accelerating the counteraction.

chapters.title: Controlling the Angle in Partner Practice
chapters.summary: During independent practice, participants refine the point angle, torso rotation, buckler work, and stepping direction.
chapters.anchor: Better start with parry riposte.
theses: Raising the arm too high opens the torso and makes the thrusting direction unclear.
The shoulder and torso must contribute rather than staying fixed while only the arms move.
After contact, the fencer can continue with another thrust or switch to a cut at the arm or leg if the opponent withdraws quickly.

chapters.title: Break Before the Final Section
chapters.summary: The group removes masks, loosens equipment, drinks water, and prepares for the last part of the seminar.
chapters.anchor: Guys, now please put down your masks.
theses: The break separates technical work on the inside-line thrust from the final tactical section.
Participants are given time to cool down and restore their attention.

chapters.title: Invitation with a Short Half-Step
chapters.summary: A short preparation with the buckler lowered provokes a reaction and creates an opportunity for a counterattack or parry-riposte.
chapters.anchor: okay uh now uh we talking about uh another one concept
theses: Against a highly defensive weapon system, preparing the action matters more than relying on speed alone.
The half-step and open line act as an invitation, not a commitment to complete the feint as an attack.
If the opponent does not react, the preparation is repeated or abandoned; the deception is not expected to work every time.

chapters.title: Descending and Rising Thrusts
chapters.summary: The group first completes the sequence with a descending thrust, then uses a low threat to move the buckler and open a line for a rising thrust to the torso.
chapters.anchor: This is the last exercise for upward thrust
theses: The descending thrust completes the previous sequence with a threat to the arm or thigh.
The low threat must be credible enough to make the opponent lower the buckler.
The sequence is first practiced as a parry-riposte, then as a counterattack with a rising thrust.
A short step gives time to read the reaction without turning the preparation into an uncontrolled lunge.

chapters.title: The Reach of a Thrust to the Torso
chapters.summary: The instructor explains the value of a prepared torso thrust through distance geometry and its effect on scoring.
chapters.anchor: I need a little more of your attention.
theses: The opponent may cover the head or have a height advantage, so the upper target is not automatically available.
A hit to the leg scores less, while two prepared thrusts can change the score quickly.
Geometrically, a thrust to the torso can reach farther than a cut to the knee.

chapters.title: Disengagement and the Inside-Line Thrust
chapters.summary: Participants lift the partner’s blade, disengage, and guide the point in an arc toward the inside line.
chapters.anchor: So, let us do an exercise.
theses: The disengagement opens the line for a thrust after blade contact.
The grip gradually turns toward a flat-blade position, creating an additional angle.
The arc is practiced slowly and taken to extreme positions only as a learning exploration.

chapters.title: Flat-Blade Grip Around the Buckler
chapters.summary: Adjusting the grip and path helps the point move around the buckler without drifting far from the target.
chapters.anchor: Show me again your grip.
theses: Turning the blade flat makes it easier to create a thrusting angle on the other side of the defense.
The hand and sword move in an arc around an almost stationary point.
If the buckler presses inward, the additional angle still allows the thrust to finish.

chapters.title: One Technique in Attack and Defense
chapters.summary: The final drill transfers the same mechanics among parry-riposte, counterattack, and a prepared thrusting attack.
chapters.anchor: let's go to the very last exercise
theses: The imbroccata is used both defensively against an entry and as a continuation of the fencer’s own attack.
Preparatory cuts draw the buckler into motion, after which a half-step and lunge open the side thrust.
A cross-step lunge reduces control and can strain the wrist, so a standard lunge is recommended for the drill.

notes.title: Seminar Structure
items: The seminar progresses from stance and coordination to action selection, then to specific thrusts and tactical preparation. Each new sequence retains the mechanics of the previous one while changing the stepping direction or the partner’s response.
The instructor distinguishes general principles from experimental solutions and does not present one grip or unusual angle as the only correct option.

notes.title: Separating the Functions of the Hands
items: The sword and buckler are treated as two independent tools: one hand can create a threat while the other closes a line or controls the blade.
Bringing the hands together remains useful in some situations, but the basic training develops independence so compound-action options are not lost.

notes.title: Distance and Direction of Movement
items: Retreating supports the parry and preserves room for the riposte; moving forward supports the counterthrust. Staying in place makes sense only when the distance is already suitable.
After landing or controlling the blade, the fencer must complete the exit: staying close leaves the opponent a response to the legs and continued pressure.

notes.title: Preparing the Thrust
items: A short half-step, an open line, and a low threat are used as testable invitations. If the opponent does not react, the action is not completed automatically.
The purpose of the invitation is to move the buckler or blade and open a line; the same mechanics can then function as a parry-riposte, counterattack, or initiated attack.

items.text: Without weapons, shift to a more frontal stance while preserving the ability to extend both hands independently.
Connect forward and backward steps with separating the hands and lightly rotating the torso, then repeat with sword and buckler.
The partner repeatedly attacks the head while the defender reads the tempo and combines buckler cover with a counterthrust.
Add a half-step back to the parry and forward movement to the counterattack while maintaining working distance.
First perform the inside-line thrust as a parry-riposte while retreating, then use the same mechanics as a forward counterattack.
From the central position, rotate the wrist, bring the blade toward the inside of the partner’s buckler, and complete the thrust with a step.
With the arm extended, change the buckler position and wrist angle while maintaining blade control and protection against the opponent’s response.
After the thrust, direct the buckler into the blade, limit the opponent’s continuation, and exit safely at once.
Use a short half-step and an open upper line to provoke a reaction, then choose a retreat, parry-riposte, or counterthrust.
Present a low threat, wait for the buckler to move, and transition into a thrust to the upper line.
Lift the partner’s blade, disengage, and guide the point in an arc into an inside-line thrust.
Apply the same mechanics in defense and attack: parry-riposte, counterattack, and a prepared thrust after a series of feints.

glossary.definition: Closing the line with the blade or buckler at the same time as one’s own attack or counterattack.
A parry followed immediately by a returning offensive action.
A descending thrust from above; in the seminar, the term serves as a reference for the inside-line trajectory.
A hand and hilt position that turns the blade flat to create an additional thrusting angle.
A fast attacking entry that continues forward; here it serves as an example of an entry addressed by the defensive technique.
An immediate renewal of the thrust or cut after the first action fails or is closed, without fully returning to the initial position.
